reason: The sources provide over 15 cross-validated claims from multiple independent websites detailing the Milky Way's scale, central supermassive black hole, orbital properties, and merger history.
story: For centuries, humans believed the Milky Way encompassed the entire universe. That changed in the 1920s when Edwin Hubble used stellar distance markers to prove distant spiral nebulae were actually separate galaxies. Today, we know our cosmic home is a barred spiral galaxy containing up to 400 billion stars. At its heart lies Sagittarius A*, a supermassive black hole over 4 million times the mass of the Sun. NASA's Chandra observatory caught Sagittarius A* unleashing a giant X-ray flare 400 times brighter than normal, likely triggered by a shredded asteroid or tangled magnetic field lines. Our Solar System orbits this central engine inside the Orion Arm at over 500,000 miles per hour, taking over 200 million years to complete one loop. Remarkably, up to half of our galaxy's matter—and the atoms inside our bodies—originally traveled from distant galaxies via powerful intergalactic winds.
angle: Up to half of the matter in the Milky Way—and the atoms inside our bodies—originally came from distant galaxies billions of years ago.

claims.claim: Until the 1920s, astronomers believed the Milky Way contained all the stars in the universe until Edwin Hubble proved other galaxies exist outside it.
Edwin Hubble measured distances using Cepheid variable stars to prove spiral nebulae were separate galaxies located far outside the Milky Way.
The Milky Way is classified as a barred spiral galaxy featuring a central bar structure.
At the center of the Milky Way lies a supermassive black hole named Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*).
Sagittarius A* contains an estimated mass of approximately 4.1 to 4.5 million solar masses.
NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory detected a record-breaking flare from Sagittarius A* that was 400 times brighter than its normal state.
Astronomers theorize the 400-times-brighter X-ray flare was caused either by an asteroid torn apart by gravity or by tangled magnetic field lines.
The Solar System is located roughly 26,000 to 30,000 light-years away from the center of the Milky Way.
The Solar System sits slightly above the central midplane of the galactic disk, with estimates ranging between 20 and 82 light-years above.
The Sun and Solar System take over 200 million years (estimated between 212 and 230 million years) to complete one orbit around the Milky Way.
The Solar System resides within a spiral structure known as the Orion Arm (or Local Arm / spur).
Dark matter is estimated to make up about 90 percent of the total mass of the Milky Way galaxy.
Up to 40 to 50 percent of the matter in the Milky Way originated from distant galaxies via intergalactic transfer.
About 11 billion years ago, the Milky Way merged with a major satellite galaxy nicknamed the Kraken.
Ancient dense star clusters known as globular clusters orbit in the Milky Way's halo and help astronomers reconstruct its galactic collision history.
Interstellar dust within the galactic plane absorbs optical light, preventing optical telescopes from peering directly through the disk to the galactic bulge.

disputed: Distance from the Sun to Galactic Center: sources give varying numbers (26,600 light-years in S4, 27,000 light-years in S1, 30,000 light-years in S6). Script should state 'roughly 26,000 to 30,000 light-years'.

Height of Solar System above the galactic plane: S4 cites standard value of 82 light-years but its own study yields 20 light-years (matching S6). Script should present the range or state 'about 20 light-years'.

Number of major spiral arms: S4 notes optical/infrared data suggests 2 main stellar arms, while radio gas observations show 4 arms. Script should attribute as 'depending on whether telescopes trace stars or interstellar gas'.

Trigger of Sgr A* 400x flare: S1 and S2 offer two competing theories (shredded asteroid vs magnetic reconnection). Script should attribute as 'astronomers suspect either a destroyed asteroid or snapped magnetic field lines'.
Ancient creation mythologies (Babylonian Tiamat dragon tail vs Greek Hera divine milk): S1 notes these are mythic stories or ancient political propaganda. Leave out of script as factual history.
